Here's a guess that's a little different from the others in the thread. Other people have mentioned that humans find comfort in finding explanations and reasons for things beyond their control, and prior to modern scientific advancement we were just doing the best we could to account for forces of nature. That's a valid point, but I also think there's a social component.

So much of religion focuses on 'here are the rules of society; if you don't adhere to these rules, bad things will happen to you'. Karma, divine retribution, damnation, what have you. I don't think that's by accident, I think it's one of the fundamental purposes of religion, actually.

Other than humans, social animals live almost entirely in single-family groups with might-makes-right hierarchies. If you're the biggest and strongest and smartest, you eat and breed first, and everyone answers to you for the things they need to survive. It's good to be the king, but it's a decreasingly appealing existence the further you go down the ladder. The ones at the very bottom are often expelled from the group or left to starve.

Some would argue that humans still live in might-makes-right societies, we've just changed the requirements to be the most powerful. And okay, fair enough, but it's at least tempered a little by the justice system, which is essentially an enforcement of morality. My neighbor probably won't come over, hit me in the eye, eat my dinner, and then sleep in my bed just because he's got a better job than me. Because now we've got laws and police and jails and so on.

But what if I was a nomad in a desert 5,000 years ago, without those benefits? I think one of the voids that religion filled in our development was convincing the mighty that they were still beholden to something. That no matter how strong you are, there's some divine entity or spiritual force that will bring down retribution on anyone that behaves in a way that's detrimental to the rest of the group. It's an important foil to have, because those that attain power in might-makes-right society are often the ones you'd least want in control.

It might have backfired from time to time. There's a quote attributed to Genghis Khan (that's actually unsourced and probably no older than the internet) about “I am the punishment of God... If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.” Whether or not he actually said it, there's plenty of people that did bad things for what they thought were good reasons. But overall, I think it allowed us to cooperate in bigger groups and improved the quality of life for the people that weren't at the top.

And I additionally think it provides comfort not just from the forces of nature but from the evil of men - if I can say "that man ruined my crops, killed my livestock, and kidnapped my children; but one day, he'll know the wrath of Dagon" then I can get on with my life.

You can make sense of pretty much any part of any religion if you just look at it in the right way. For my example I'll talk about one of the stupider rules and why it was actually brilliant. Sacred Cows in India. "Hey, stupid religious idiot. Starve to death for your religion instead of eating that cow. Ha ha, what an idiot." Well no. This is actually brilliant. Here's why:

A long time ago someone realized that cows eat useless stuff and garbage. Useless stuff - grass and weeds. Garbage - we grow wheat and take the seed and the rest of it is hay, which is garbage to humans. Cows eat this stuff and poop out fertilizer. You can put cows on some land that isn't fertile enough to grow crops for humans and after some time they will have eaten what little was growing there and pooped out enough fertilizer to make the land fertile enough for human use. And not only that, the cow could breed and make more cows that could do this to more, and more land.

You see if someone back then would kill a cow they would be able to eat for a short time. Until the meat ran out or started to rot. If they let it live, that cow would eat garbage and useless stuff until there was a field that could grow crops to feed that person for years and years. And the cows would breed and be able to do this to more and more land. All that had to be done was to not kill the cows.

So you have to make it illegal to kill cows, but that isn't going to be enough. Imagine there is a guy who is starving to death. He has a choice, starve to death or eat a cow. The worst punishment he could get is to be killed, that is if he gets caught. But you need to convince this guy not to kill it because the fertilizer and calves it produces will save many, many more lives. So you need two things to convince this guy not to do it. You need a punishment worse than death. And you need to convince this guy that no matter how sneaky he is, an all seeing eye will see him do it. So you come up with heaven and hell and an all seeing judge.

So to answer your question - "Why did early humans develop religion and gods?" Because they needed an all seeing judge (gods) and they needed a punishment worse than death (hell).

If you look at virtually any part of religion, you will see things like this. You will see reason as to why these rules were made, and the benefits that came with them. And in a lot of cases, why following these religions is or was a very good thing. People will claim that religion is stupid, "Ha ha, look at that idiot starve to death right next to a cow." But there are reasons behind these religious rules. People following these rules thrived because of them. They built empires upon these religious rules. Some rules are outdated, some rules are no longer relevant, but to decide which rules are still relevant and which aren't, we must understand why they existed in the first place.
